name: Abadie’s Sign
formal: Loss or reduction of deep pain when the Achilles tendon is squeezed firmly; classic in tabes dorsalis (dorsal column disease).
simple: Squeezing the Achilles tendon (the big tendon above the heel) hurts much less than it should. It is an old sign of nerve damage from advanced, untreated syphilis affecting the spinal cord.

name: Abducens (VI) Nerve Palsy
formal: Weak lateral rectus: impaired abduction with horizontal diplopia worse on looking to the affected side. Causes: microvascular, raised ICP (false-localizing), pontine lesion; consider myasthenia.
simple: A weak nerve to the eye muscle that turns the eye outward, so the eye cannot look fully sideways and the person sees double, worse toward the weak side; causes include small vessel disease or raised brain pressure.
aN: vi | abducens nerve palsy

name: Abductor Sign
formal: Resisted hip abduction: in organic weakness the normal leg stays still while the weak leg abducts poorly; in functional weakness the "weak" leg is pushed out (involuntary abduction) when the other leg abducts.
simple: While testing hip strength on both sides at once, a truly weak leg stays still but a non-organically weak leg pushes outward involuntarily, helping tell real nerve weakness from functional weakness.

name: Absence
formal: Brief lapse of awareness of epileptic origin, with staring and sudden onset/offset, usually without post-ictal confusion.
simple: A short seizure where a person suddenly blanks out and stares for a few seconds, then just as suddenly returns to normal, usually with no confusion afterward.

name: Abulia
formal: Loss of initiative, spontaneity and drive with apathy and slowed responses; frontal–subcortical (e.g. ACA territory, caudate) lesions.
simple: A loss of motivation and initiative, where a person becomes apathetic, does not start things on their own, and responds slowly, often from damage to the front of the brain or nearby structures.

name: Acalculia
formal: Acquired difficulty with calculation; dominant parietal (angular gyrus) lesions, part of Gerstmann syndrome.
simple: A learned difficulty doing simple math after brain damage, usually from a stroke in a specific part of the left side of the brain used for numbers.

name: Achromatopsia
formal: Acquired loss of colour perception (cerebral), usually from bilateral ventral occipitotemporal (fusiform) lesions.
simple: Losing the ability to see colors after a brain injury, everything looks gray, usually from damage to color-processing areas on both sides of the brain.

name: Adson’s Test
formal: Arm extended and externally rotated, neck extended and turned to the tested side with deep inspiration; loss of the radial pulse / reproduction of symptoms suggests vascular thoracic outlet syndrome.
simple: The arm is stretched and rotated while the neck turns and tilts back with a deep breath in. If the wrist pulse fades or symptoms return, it suggests a vessel or nerve pinched near the neck and shoulder.

name: Age-Related Signs
formal: Findings that can be normal in older people, e.g. reduced ankle jerks, reduced vibration at the toes, reduced upgaze; interpret with caution.
simple: Certain findings, like weaker ankle reflexes, less vibration sense in the toes, or trouble looking upward, can simply be normal aging rather than disease, so doctors interpret them cautiously in older patients.

name: Ageusia
formal: Loss of taste; consider chorda tympani / facial nerve, brainstem (nucleus of the solitary tract) or olfactory causes.
simple: Complete loss of the sense of taste, which can come from damage to specific taste nerves, a brainstem problem, or loss of smell (which affects flavor).

name: Agnosopsia
formal: Accurate visual perceptual judgments despite denial of seeing ("knowing without seeing"); related to blindsight after occipital damage.
simple: A rare condition where a person can accurately judge or respond to something they see, while insisting they cannot see it at all. It resembles blindsight and follows damage to the vision part of the brain.

name: Agnosia
formal: Failure to recognise stimuli in one modality despite intact primary sensation, attention and language.
simple: An inability to recognize familiar things (objects, faces, sounds) through one particular sense, even though that sense itself and language and attention are working fine.

name: Agrammatism
formal: Speech reduced to content words with loss of grammatical words and inflections; non-fluent (Broca-type) aphasia.
simple: Speech that drops the small connecting words (like "the," "is," endings) and comes out as strings of nouns and verbs. It is a feature of a type of language problem after a stroke that also makes speech non-fluent.

name: Agraphia
formal: Acquired disorder of writing; may be aphasic, apraxic, spatial or part of Gerstmann syndrome.
simple: A newly acquired problem with writing, which can occur alongside language, movement-planning, or spatial problems after brain injury.

name: Agrypnia (Excitata)
formal: Severe persistent insomnia, e.g. fatal familial insomnia, Morvan syndrome.
simple: A severe, unrelenting inability to sleep, seen in rare conditions like fatal familial insomnia or Morvan syndrome, where the body's normal sleep-wake control breaks down.
aN: excitata | agrypnia

name: Akathisia
formal: Subjective inner restlessness with an urge to move and repetitive shifting of posture; often drug-induced (dopamine blockers).
simple: An uncomfortable inner restlessness that makes a person feel they must keep moving, shifting position, or pacing. It is often a side effect of medications that block dopamine.

name: Akinesia
formal: Absence or poverty of voluntary movement, difficulty initiating movement; parkinsonism.
simple: A poverty or slowness of movement where it becomes hard to start moving at all, a core feature of Parkinson's disease and related conditions.

name: Akinetic Mutism
formal: Awake-appearing patient with eyes open who does not move or speak spontaneously; bilateral frontal/cingulate or mesodiencephalic lesions.
simple: A state where the patient appears awake with eyes open but does not move or speak on their own, from damage to the front of the brain or deep midline brain structures.

name: Akinetopsia
formal: Selective inability to perceive motion (motion blindness); lateral occipitotemporal (V5/MT) lesions.
simple: A rare condition where a person cannot perceive motion, moving objects appear as a series of disconnected still images, from damage to a specific motion-processing brain area.

name: Alalia
formal: Obsolete term for loss of the ability to transform ideas into speech sounds (aphasia after stroke).
simple: An old-fashioned word for losing the ability to turn thoughts into spoken words, essentially what is now called aphasia after a stroke.

name: Alexia
formal: Acquired inability to read; pure alexia (without agraphia) from left occipital + splenium lesions.
simple: An acquired inability to read after brain damage, even though the person can still write, due to a stroke affecting the connections between the eyes' visual input and language areas.

name: Alexithymia
formal: Reduced ability to identify and describe one's own emotions.
simple: Difficulty noticing and putting words to one's own emotions.

name: Alice in Wonderland Syndrome
formal: Distorted perception of body image, size or shape of objects (micropsia/macropsia); migraine, epilepsy, EBV infection.
simple: A perceptual disturbance where a person's own body or objects around them seem to shrink or grow in size, seen with migraine, epilepsy, or certain viral infections.

name: Alien Grasp Reflex
formal: Involuntary grasping by the alien hand; frontal (SMA / corpus callosum) lesions, corticobasal syndrome.
simple: An involuntary grabbing reflex of one hand that the person cannot control, from damage to the planning or connecting areas at the front of the brain.

name: Alien Hand, Alien Limb
formal: Limb performs complex purposeful-looking movements the patient does not feel in control of; corticobasal syndrome, callosal or frontal lesions.
simple: A limb performs seemingly purposeful movements that the person feels are not under their own control, seen with certain brain diseases affecting the frontal lobes or the connection between brain hemispheres.
aN: alien hand | alien limb

name: Alloacousia
formal: Auditory form of neglect: voices from the contralesional side are ignored or attributed to the opposite side; marker of unilateral spatial neglect.
simple: A form of inattention where a person ignores or mislocates sounds coming from one side, as if all sounds were coming from the other, unaffected side, part of one-sided neglect after a stroke.

name: Alloaesthesia
formal: Misplacement of a sensory stimulus to another location, often contralateral; right parietal lesions with neglect.
simple: A touch or pain on one side of the body is mistakenly felt as happening somewhere else, often on the opposite side, usually from a stroke causing neglect of one side.

name: Allochiria
formal: A stimulus on one side is perceived at the corresponding point on the opposite side; parietal / spinal lesions.
simple: Touch on one side is felt at the mirror-image spot on the other side; caused by a brain or spinal cord lesion.

name: Allographia
formal: Mixing of letter forms (e.g. upper and lower case) or substitution of letters when writing.
simple: Mixing up letter styles when writing, such as switching between capital and lowercase letters randomly, or substituting the wrong letters.

name: Allokinesia, Allokinesis
formal: Movement of the wrong limb (often the opposite side) when asked to move one limb; neglect syndromes.
simple: When asked to move one limb, the person moves the wrong one instead, often the opposite limb, seen in neglect after brain injury.
aN: allokinesia | allokinesis

name: Altitudinal Field Defect
formal: Loss of the upper or lower half of the visual field respecting the horizontal meridian; typically anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, retinal vascular occlusion.
simple: Loss of vision in the upper or lower half of the visual field with a sharp horizontal cutoff, typically from a blocked blood vessel affecting the eye's optic nerve or retina.

name: Amaurosis
formal: Visual loss; amaurosis fugax = transient monocular blindness, often carotid embolic.
simple: Loss of vision. A brief version, called amaurosis fugax, is a temporary episode of blindness in one eye, often from a small clot passing through an artery in the neck.

name: Amnesia
formal: Impairment of episodic memory — anterograde (new learning) and/or retrograde; medial temporal / diencephalic lesions.
simple: Impaired memory for recent experiences, either trouble forming new memories going forward or trouble recalling ones from before the problem started, usually from damage to memory-related brain structures.

name: Amphigory
formal: Nonsense speech — fluent but meaningless utterances (Miller Fisher).
simple: Speech that flows smoothly but makes no real sense, seen in a rare condition called Miller Fisher syndrome.

name: Amusia
formal: Loss of ability to perceive (receptive) or produce (expressive) music.
simple: Acquired inability to enjoy, recognise or make music — tunes may sound like noise or singing becomes impossible.

name: Amyotrophy
formal: Muscle wasting from neurogenic causes (e.g. neuralgic amyotrophy, diabetic amyotrophy, ALS).
simple: Muscle wasting caused by damage to the nerves that supply the muscle, rather than to the muscle itself, seen in conditions like ALS or certain diabetic nerve disorders.

name: Analgesia
formal: Loss of pain sensation.
simple: A complete loss of the ability to feel pain.

name: Anal Reflex
formal: Contraction of the external anal sphincter on perianal pinprick (anal wink), S2–S4; lost in cauda equina / conus lesions.
simple: A brief squeeze of the anal opening when the skin around it is lightly pricked, testing the lowest nerves of the spinal cord; its absence suggests damage to the lower spinal cord or its nerve roots.

name: Anarthria
formal: Complete inability to articulate speech (most severe dysarthria); e.g. locked-in syndrome, bilateral opercular lesions.
simple: A complete inability to form spoken words due to severe weakness or paralysis of the muscles used for speech, the most extreme form of slurred speech, as seen in locked-in syndrome.

name: Angioscotoma
formal: Scotoma corresponding to retinal blood vessel shadows.
simple: A blind spot in vision that follows the shadow pattern cast by blood vessels inside the eye, a normal optical finding rather than disease.

name: Angor Animi
formal: Sense of impending death; may occur on waking or as a somaesthetic migraine aura, also in angina.
simple: An intense feeling that death is near or imminent, which can occur on waking, during a certain type of migraine aura, or with a heart attack.

name: Anhidrosis
formal: Absence of sweating; sympathetic pathway (e.g. Horner), small-fibre neuropathy or autonomic failure.
simple: An absence of normal sweating in part of the body, usually from damage to the nerves that control sweat glands, such as in Horner's syndrome or certain nerve diseases.

name: Anismus
formal: Paradoxical contraction of the anal sphincter / puborectalis on attempted defecation; may be dystonic (e.g. Parkinson's).
simple: An inability to relax the anal muscles properly during a bowel movement, causing straining; it can be linked to conditions like Parkinson's disease.

name: Anisocoria
formal: Unequal pupil size; compare in light and dark to decide which pupil is abnormal (Horner vs III nerve / pharmacological).
simple: One pupil is a different size from the other. Doctors check the pupils in both light and dark rooms to figure out which one is abnormal and why.

name: Annular Scotoma
formal: Ring-shaped scotoma around fixation; retinitis pigmentosa, glaucoma, vitamin A deficiency.
simple: A ring-shaped blind area in vision surrounding the point a person is looking at, seen in conditions like retinitis pigmentosa or glaucoma.

name: Anosmia
formal: Loss of smell; head injury, olfactory groove meningioma, neurodegenerative disease (PD), post-viral.
simple: A complete loss of the sense of smell, which can follow head injury, certain brain tumors, viral infections, or early Parkinson's disease.

name: Anosodiaphoria
formal: Indifference to a neurological deficit that is acknowledged; right hemisphere lesions.
simple: A person acknowledges they have a neurological problem, such as a paralyzed limb, but seems strangely unconcerned about it, seen after damage to the right side of the brain.

name: Anosognosia
formal: Unawareness or denial of a neurological deficit (e.g. hemiplegia); typically right parietal lesions.
simple: A person is unaware of, or denies having, an obvious neurological problem such as paralysis on one side, usually from damage to the right side of the brain.

name: Anserina
formal: "Goose-flesh" skin: autonomic piloerection and cold, bumpy skin.
simple: Goosebumps: the skin becomes cold, bumpy, and hair stands up, a normal reflex of the body's automatic nervous system.

name: Antecollis
formal: Forward flexion of the neck (dystonic or axial rigidity); MSA, PD, myopathy.
simple: The neck bends forward involuntarily and stays that way, seen in some movement disorders like multiple system atrophy or Parkinson's disease.

name: Anteflexion
formal: Forward flexion of the trunk; see camptocormia.
simple: The whole trunk bends forward, related to a condition called camptocormia.

name: Anton’s Syndrome
formal: Cortical blindness with denial of blindness (visual anosognosia) ± confabulation; bilateral PCA territory (occipital) lesions.
simple: A person is completely blind from brain damage but firmly denies it, sometimes even making up descriptions of things they cannot actually see, from damage to the vision centers on both sides of the brain.

name: Anwesenheit
formal: Feeling of a presence nearby (sense of presence); PD, epilepsy, migraine.
simple: A vivid feeling that someone or something is present nearby even though no one is actually there, reported in Parkinson's disease, epilepsy, or migraine.

name: Apathy
formal: Reduced motivation, initiative and emotional responsiveness; frontal–subcortical dysfunction.
simple: A loss of motivation, interest, and emotional reaction to things, linked to dysfunction in the front part of the brain and its connections.

name: Aphantasia
formal: Absence of voluntary visual imagery ("mind's eye" blindness); congenital or acquired.
simple: An inability to voluntarily picture images in one's mind (no "mind's eye"), which can be present from birth or appear after a brain injury.

name: Aphemia
formal: Severe loss of speech output (Broca's original term); now used for pure motor speech loss with preserved writing.
simple: A severe loss of the ability to speak while the ability to write remains intact, from damage to a specific speech-motor area of the brain.

name: Aphonia
formal: Loss of voice (no phonation); laryngeal, vagal or functional causes.
simple: A complete loss of the voice, so no sound can be produced, from problems with the voice box, the nerve supplying it, or sometimes stress-related causes.

name: Aposiopesis
formal: Sentences begun but left unfinished; aphasia of dementia.
simple: Sentences that trail off and are left unfinished, a speech pattern sometimes seen in dementia.

name: Applause Sign
formal: Claps more than three times when asked to clap three times quickly; PSP and other frontal-subcortical disorders.
simple: Asked to clap just three times, the person cannot stop at three. Typical of PSP and other frontal-subcortical conditions.

name: Aprosexia
formal: Inability to maintain attention.
simple: An inability to focus or sustain attention on anything.

name: Aprosodia, Aprosody
formal: Loss of melody, rhythm and emotional tone of speech (expressive) or of understanding it (receptive); right hemisphere lesions.
simple: A loss of the normal melody, rhythm, and emotional tone of speech, either being unable to express emotion through tone of voice or being unable to detect it in others' voices, from damage to the right side of the brain.
aN: aprosodia | aprosody

name: Arcuate Scotoma
formal: Arc-shaped scotoma from the blind spot following nerve fibre bundles; glaucoma, optic nerve lesions.
simple: A curved, arc-shaped blind spot in vision that follows the path of nerve fibers from the blind spot, typically seen in glaucoma or optic nerve damage.

name: Argyll Robertson Pupil (ARP)
formal: Small irregular pupils that do not react to light but constrict to accommodation (light–near dissociation); neurosyphilis, diabetes.
simple: Small, irregular pupils that fail to shrink to bright light but still shrink normally when focusing up close. This unusual pattern is classically linked to untreated syphilis or diabetes.
aN: arp | argyll robertson pupil

name: Asemasia
formal: Inability to communicate by signs or speech, including gesture and pantomime (broader than aphasia).
simple: An inability to communicate at all through speech, gestures, or signs, a broader and more severe problem than typical language loss (aphasia).

name: Asomatognosia
formal: Lack of awareness of, or denial of ownership of, a part of the body; right parietal lesions.
simple: A person fails to recognize, or denies owning, a part of their own body (commonly an arm or leg), usually after damage to the right side of the brain.

name: Astasia-Abasia
formal: Inability to stand or walk with preserved leg power in bed; functional gait, or midline cerebellar / frontal disorders.
simple: A person cannot stand or walk steadily even though their leg muscles test as strong when lying in bed. It is often seen in non-organic (functional) gait problems, though some brain conditions can cause it too.

name: Asterixis
formal: Negative myoclonus: brief lapses of posture producing flapping of outstretched dorsiflexed hands; metabolic encephalopathy (hepatic, uremic, CO2).
simple: A brief, repeated loss of muscle tone causing the outstretched hands to flap when the wrists are held bent back. It signals a metabolic problem affecting the brain, such as liver or kidney failure.

name: Asthenopia
formal: Eye strain from uncorrected refractive error or convergence insufficiency; headache/eye ache with near work.
simple: Eye strain, tiredness, or aching, usually from uncorrected glasses prescription or from difficulty focusing both eyes together on close work.

name: Asynergia
formal: Loss of coordination between muscle groups in complex movements; cerebellar.
simple: A loss of smooth coordination between different muscle groups needed for a complex movement, a feature of cerebellum (balance-center) problems.

name: Ataxia
formal: Incoordination of movement not due to weakness: cerebellar, sensory (proprioceptive) or vestibular.
simple: Clumsy, uncoordinated movements not caused by muscle weakness. It can come from a problem in the cerebellum (balance center), the nerves carrying position sense, or the inner ear balance system.

name: Ataxic Hemiparesis
formal: Lacunar syndrome: ipsilateral weakness (leg > arm) with cerebellar-type ataxia; internal capsule / pons.
simple: A pattern of stroke causing weakness down one side of the body (worse in the leg than the arm) combined with clumsy, uncoordinated movement on that same side, typically from a small deep stroke.

name: Athymhormia
formal: Severe loss of self-activation ("robot syndrome"): inert unless prompted, but performs normally when stimulated; bilateral basal ganglia/frontal lesions.
simple: A severe loss of self-driven activity, sometimes called "robot syndrome," where a person does nothing unless prompted but can perform tasks normally once given a cue, from damage deep in both sides of the brain.

name: Atrophy
formal: Wasting of muscle or other tissue; neurogenic, myopathic or disuse.
simple: Wasting or shrinking of muscle or other body tissue, which can happen from nerve damage, muscle disease, or simply from disuse.

name: Attended Alone Sign
formal: Patient attends a memory clinic without a companion — suggests functional (subjective) memory complaint rather than dementia.
simple: A patient comes to a memory clinic appointment alone, without family or friends. This pattern more often points to worry about memory rather than true dementia, since dementia patients are usually brought by a companion.

name: Attention
formal: Ability to focus and sustain awareness; tested with digit span, serial 7s, months backward.
simple: The ability to focus on and keep track of information, commonly tested by asking someone to repeat a string of numbers, count backward by sevens, or say the months in reverse order.

name: Auditory Agnosia
formal: Inability to recognise sounds with preserved hearing; bilateral temporal lesions.
simple: An inability to recognize familiar sounds despite hearing being intact, from damage to sound-processing areas on both sides of the brain.

name: Auditory-Visual Synaesthesia
formal: Sounds evoke visual sensations (photisms); optic nerve / chiasmal lesions or congenital synesthesia.
simple: Sounds trigger visual sensations, such as flashes of light, either as a lifelong trait or from a problem with the eye's nerve or visual pathway.

name: Augmentation
formal: (1) Increase in strength after brief voluntary contraction in LEMS; (2) earlier/more severe restless legs symptoms on dopaminergic therapy.
simple: Two meanings: strength briefly improving right after a voluntary contraction in a nerve-muscle disorder called Lambert-Eaton syndrome, or restless legs symptoms starting earlier with certain Parkinson's medications.

name: Aura
formal: Subjective warning symptom at the onset of a seizure or migraine.
simple: A warning sensation felt right before a seizure or migraine begins, such as a strange smell, visual flickering, or a feeling of unease.

name: Automatic Obedience
formal: Excessive compliance with the examiner's instructions or manipulation; catatonia, frontal lesions.
simple: A person follows the examiner's instructions or physical repositioning excessively and without resistance, seen in catatonia or certain frontal brain lesions.

name: Automatism
formal: Involuntary stereotyped actions (lip smacking, fumbling) during impaired awareness; complex partial seizures.
simple: Repeated, purposeless actions like lip-smacking or fidgeting that happen while a person's awareness is impaired, typically during a certain type of seizure.

name: Autophony
formal: Hearing one's own voice and breathing abnormally loudly; patulous Eustachian tube, superior canal dehiscence.
simple: Hearing one's own voice or breathing unusually loudly inside the head, usually from a problem with the ear's air pressure tube or a defect in the inner ear bone.

name: Autoscopy
formal: Seeing an image of one's own body in external space; temporoparietal junction dysfunction.
simple: Seeing an image or double of one's own body as if standing outside oneself, linked to dysfunction where the brain's vision and body-sense areas meet.

name: Autotopagnosia
formal: Inability to localise or name parts of one's own body; left parietal lesions.
simple: An inability to point to, name, or recognize parts of one's own body on command, from damage to the left side of the brain.

name: Babinski’s Sign (2)
formal: Paradoxical elevation of the eyebrow on the side of hemifacial spasm when the eye closes (other Babinski sign); distinguishes hemifacial spasm from blepharospasm.
simple: When the eye closes during an involuntary facial spasm, the eyebrow on that same side lifts up instead of staying still, helping tell that specific spasm apart from ordinary eyelid twitching.
aN: 2 | babinski sign

name: Babinski’s Trunk-Thigh Test
formal: Supine patient sits up with arms crossed: the paretic leg lifts involuntarily (organic hemiparesis); both legs or healthy leg lift in functional weakness.
simple: Lying down with arms crossed, the patient tries to sit up. One leg lifting off the bed suggests true weakness on that side; both legs, or the healthy leg lifting, suggests non-organic weakness.

name: Balaclava Helmet
formal: Distribution of facial sensory loss sparing the central face (onion-skin), from spinal trigeminal nucleus lesions, e.g. syringobulbia.
simple: A pattern of facial numbness that spares the very center of the face but affects the outer parts like a ski mask, from damage to a specific nerve pathway in the brainstem or upper spinal cord.

name: Balint’s Syndrome
formal: Simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and ocular apraxia; bilateral parieto-occipital lesions.
simple: Three problems from damage to both sides of the back of the brain: seeing only one object at a time in a busy scene, trouble reaching accurately for things by sight, and difficulty aiming the eyes where one wants.

name: Battle’s Sign
formal: Bruising over the mastoid process; sign of basal (middle cranial fossa) skull fracture.
simple: Bruising that appears behind the ear over the bone, a warning sign of a fracture at the base of the skull.

name: Bell’s Palsy
formal: Idiopathic acute LMN facial palsy involving the forehead.
simple: A sudden, one-sided facial weakness of unknown cause that affects the whole side of the face, including the forehead, because the facial nerve itself is not working.

name: Bell’s Phenomenon, Bell’s Sign
formal: Upward (and outward) deviation of the eye on attempted eye closure; visible in LMN facial palsy; preserved in supranuclear gaze palsy.
simple: When trying to close the eye, the eyeball rolls upward and outward instead of the lid closing properly. It becomes visible when the eyelid is too weak to close, from facial nerve damage.
aN: bell phenomenon | bell sign

name: Benediction Hand
formal: Inability to flex index and middle fingers on making a fist (median nerve lesion) — or posture from ulnar lesion at rest.
simple: An inability to bend the index and middle fingers when making a fist, so the hand looks like giving a blessing, caused by damage to the wrist's median nerve; a similar posture can occur with ulnar nerve damage.

name: Bielschowsky’s Sign, Bielschowsky’s Test
formal: Head tilt test: hypertropia increases on tilting the head toward the side of a superior oblique (IV nerve) palsy.
simple: Tilting the head to one side makes one eye drift noticeably higher than the other; the drift gets worse when tilting toward the side of a weak eye muscle, helping pinpoint which small eye-movement nerve is affected.
aN: bielschowsky sign | bielschowsky test

name: Blepharospasm
formal: Focal dystonia with involuntary forced eye closure.
simple: Involuntary, forceful squeezing shut of the eyelids, caused by a type of muscle spasm disorder called dystonia.

name: Blindsight
formal: Residual ability to detect/localise visual stimuli in a cortically blind field without conscious awareness; occipital (V1) lesions.
simple: A person blind from brain damage can still unconsciously detect or point toward things in their blind field, even though they report seeing nothing, from damage to the main vision-processing brain area.

name: Blind Spot
formal: Physiological scotoma corresponding to the optic disc; enlarged in papilledema.
simple: The small normal area in everyone's vision where the optic nerve exits the eye and there are no light-sensing cells; it becomes larger than normal when there is swelling of the optic nerve from raised brain pressure.

name: Blinking
formal: Spontaneous blink rate: reduced in PD/PSP, increased in blepharospasm, Tourette syndrome.
simple: How often someone blinks on their own can be informative: fewer blinks than normal occurs in Parkinson's disease, while more frequent blinking can occur in eyelid spasm disorders or Tourette syndrome.

name: Blink Reflex
formal: Reflex eye closure to stimulation (glabellar, corneal, supraorbital, auditory, visual threat).
simple: The automatic closing of the eyes in response to a stimulus like a tap on the forehead, a touch on the cornea, a loud sound, or something suddenly approaching the eye.

name: Bon-Bon Sign
formal: Tongue pushed into the cheek producing a bulge (like a sweet) — orolingual dyskinesia, tardive dyskinesia.
simple: The tongue pushes against the inside of the cheek, making it bulge out like there is candy in the mouth, an involuntary movement often caused by certain medications affecting the brain's movement control.

name: Bouche De Tapir
formal: Pouting protrusion of the lips from facial (orbicularis) weakness; facioscapulohumeral dystrophy.
simple: The lips stick out in a pouting shape because the muscles around the mouth are weak, seen in a muscle disease called facioscapulohumeral dystrophy.

name: Bovine Cough
formal: Weak cough without the explosive start due to vocal cord paralysis (recurrent laryngeal nerve).
simple: A weak cough that lacks the usual sharp, explosive burst at the start, because the vocal cords are not closing properly due to a damaged nerve in the voice box.

name: Bradylalia
formal: Abnormally slow speech.
simple: Speaking unusually slowly.

name: Bradyphrenia
formal: Slowness of thought processing; subcortical dementia, parkinsonism.
simple: Slowed thinking, where it takes longer than normal to process information and respond, seen in Parkinson's disease and related conditions.

name: Brueghel’s Syndrome
formal: Oromandibular (jaw-opening) dystonia with involuntary mouth opening.
simple: A muscle spasm disorder causing the jaw to pull open involuntarily.

name: Bruit
formal: Vascular murmur heard over an artery (carotid, orbit, skull) — stenosis or AV fistula/malformation.
simple: A whooshing or humming sound heard with a stethoscope over a blood vessel, which can indicate narrowing of the artery or an abnormal connection between blood vessels.

name: Brushfield Spots
formal: Small grey-white spots at the periphery of the iris; Down syndrome (also normal).
simple: Small light-colored spots scattered around the edge of the colored part of the eye (iris), commonly seen in Down syndrome but also found in some people without it.

name: Bruxism
formal: Grinding or clenching of the teeth, awake or in sleep.
simple: Grinding or clenching the teeth, which can happen while awake or during sleep.

name: Buccolingual Syndrome
formal: Tardive dyskinesia of the mouth and tongue: chewing, lip smacking, tongue protrusion.
simple: Repetitive, involuntary chewing, lip-smacking, and tongue-poking movements, a type of side effect from long-term use of certain psychiatric medications.

name: Bulbar Palsy
formal: LMN weakness of muscles supplied by the lower cranial nerves: flaccid dysarthria, dysphagia, wasted fasciculating tongue, absent gag.
simple: Weakness of the muscles controlled by the lower nerves coming out of the brainstem, causing slurred, breathy speech, trouble swallowing, a wasted twitching tongue, and a weak gag reflex.

name: Bulbocavernosus Reflex
formal: Contraction of bulbocavernosus/anal sphincter on squeezing the glans or clitoris (S2–S4); lost in conus/cauda equina lesions.
simple: A brief muscle contraction around the anus when the tip of the penis or clitoris is squeezed, testing the lowest nerves of the spinal cord; it is lost with damage to the lower spinal cord or its nerve roots.

name: Buphthalmos
formal: Enlarged globe from congenital glaucoma ("ox eye").
simple: An abnormally enlarged eyeball present from birth, caused by increased pressure inside the eye (congenital glaucoma).

name: Cacogeusia
formal: Unpleasant, foul taste perception; seizures, dental or drug causes.
simple: An unpleasant or foul taste sensation that is not actually caused by food, which can occur with seizures, dental problems, or certain medications.

name: Calf Head Sign
formal: With arms raised (shoulders abducted, elbows flexed 90°) the pattern of wasted/enlarged arm muscles looks like "calf heads"; dysferlinopathy (Miyoshi).
simple: When the arms are raised with elbows bent, uneven wasting and bulging of the arm muscles gives them a lumpy shape resembling calves' heads, a finding in a specific inherited muscle disease.

name: Calf Hypertrophy
formal: Enlarged calves (pseudohypertrophy) in Duchenne/Becker dystrophy; true hypertrophy in myotonia congenita.
simple: Enlarged calf muscles that, in diseases like Duchenne muscular dystrophy, are actually filled with fat and scar tissue rather than true muscle, though in some other conditions the enlargement is real muscle.

name: Caloric Testing
formal: Irrigation of the ear canal with cold/warm water to test the vestibulo-ocular reflex; used in coma and vestibular assessment.
simple: Squirting cold or warm water into the ear canal to test how the eyes reflexively move in response, used to assess balance nerve function or to check brain function in a comatose patient.

name: Camptocormia
formal: Marked forward flexion of the trunk when standing/walking that disappears lying down; PD, dystonia, axial myopathy.
simple: A marked forward stooping of the trunk that appears when standing or walking but disappears when lying down, seen in Parkinson's disease and some muscle or movement disorders.

name: Camptodactyly
formal: Fixed flexion deformity of fingers (usually little finger).
simple: A finger, usually the little finger, that is permanently bent and cannot be fully straightened.

name: Capgras Syndrome
formal: Delusion that a familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor; DLB, Alzheimer's, right hemisphere lesions, psychosis.
simple: A false belief that a close family member or friend has been replaced by an identical impostor, seen in certain dementias, right-brain damage, or psychiatric illness.

name: Catalepsy
formal: Maintenance of limb postures imposed by the examiner (waxy flexibility); catatonia.
simple: The limbs stay in whatever position they are placed by an examiner, like a bendable wax doll, seen in catatonia.

name: Catatonia
formal: Syndrome of stupor, mutism, posturing, negativism, catalepsy and echophenomena; psychiatric or organic causes.
simple: A cluster of symptoms including being unresponsive, not speaking, holding unusual postures, resisting movement, and repeating others' words or actions, which can have psychiatric or medical causes.

name: Central Scotoma, Centrocaecal Scotoma
formal: Scotoma at fixation (± extending to the blind spot); optic neuritis, toxic/nutritional or hereditary optic neuropathy, maculopathy.
simple: A blind spot right at the point of focus, sometimes stretching to the eye's natural blind spot, commonly caused by inflammation or damage to the optic nerve or a problem with the macula (the eye's central vision area).
aN: central scotoma | centrocecal scotoma

name: Cerebellar Syndromes
formal: Ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, nystagmus, dysarthria and hypotonia; midline vs hemispheric patterns.
simple: Features of cerebellum (balance-center) damage: clumsy coordination, overshooting when reaching for things, trouble with rapid alternating movements, shaky tremor on reaching, jerky eye movements, and slurred speech.

name: Chaddock’s Sign
formal: Stroking the lateral side of the foot around the malleolus produces an extensor plantar response; corticospinal tract lesion.
simple: Stroking the skin around the outer ankle bone makes the big toe point upward, an alternative way to detect the same abnormal reflex as the classic Babinski sign, indicating damage to the brain's motor pathway.

name: Charcot Joint
formal: Painless, destroyed, unstable joint from loss of pain/proprioception (tabes, diabetes, syringomyelia).
simple: A joint that becomes painlessly destroyed and unstable because the person cannot feel pain or position sense in it, seen in advanced diabetes, syphilis, or a spinal cord condition called syringomyelia.

name: Charles Bonnet Syndrome
formal: Complex visual hallucinations with insight in people with visual loss.
simple: Detailed, vivid visual hallucinations experienced by people who have significant vision loss, while they fully understand the images are not real.

name: Chronognosia
formal: Disturbed sense of the passage of time; deep temporal/diencephalic lesions, Alzheimer's.
simple: A disturbed sense of how much time has passed, seen with certain deep brain lesions or Alzheimer's disease.

name: Chvostek’s Sign
formal: Tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear produces twitching of facial muscles; hypocalcemia (latent tetany).
simple: Tapping the cheek in front of the ear makes the facial muscles twitch, a sign of low blood calcium levels causing increased nerve excitability.

name: Ciliospinal Response
formal: Pupillary dilatation on pinching the neck skin; tests the sympathetic pathway (lost in Horner) and brainstem in coma.
simple: Pinching the skin on the side of the neck makes the pupil widen, a test of the sympathetic nervous system pathway (which is faulty in Horner's syndrome) and also used to check brainstem function in unconscious patients.

name: Clapham’s Sign
formal: Facial muscles contract when the cheek is stretched despite facial nerve palsy — preserved muscle excitation-contraction.
simple: Even with facial nerve weakness, stretching the cheek causes the facial muscle underneath to contract, showing the muscle itself can still be triggered directly even though the nerve signal is impaired.

name: Clasp-Knife Phenomenon
formal: Resistance to passive stretch that suddenly gives way; spasticity (UMN).
simple: When a limb is bent by an examiner, it initially resists strongly then suddenly gives way, like opening a pocketknife, a sign of increased muscle tone from damage to the brain's motor control pathways.

name: Claudication
formal: Pain with exercise relieved by rest; neurogenic (lumbar stenosis) vs vascular; jaw claudication in giant cell arteritis.
simple: Pain brought on by walking that eases with rest. It can come from poor blood flow to the legs or pinched nerves in the lower back; jaw pain with chewing can warn of an artery inflammation disease in older adults.

name: Claw Foot
formal: Pes cavus with clawing of the toes; hereditary neuropathy, Friedreich ataxia.
simple: A high-arched foot with the toes curled downward, seen in certain inherited nerve diseases.

name: Claw Hand
formal: Hyperextension at MCP and flexion at IP joints of the fingers; ulnar (4th/5th) or combined ulnar–median / T1 lesions.
simple: The fingers are bent at the middle and end joints while overextended at the knuckles, giving a claw-like shape, caused by damage to a nerve (usually the ulnar nerve) that controls small hand muscles.

name: Closed Fist Sign
formal: Paraesthesia in the median distribution after keeping a fist closed 60 s; provocative test for carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: Keeping the hand clenched in a fist for about a minute brings on tingling in the thumb-side fingers, a test used to help diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome (a pinched wrist nerve).

name: Closing-In Sign
formal: Copying a figure very close to or overlapping the model; Alzheimer's disease, frontal/visuospatial dysfunction.
simple: When copying a drawing, the person draws their copy very close to, or right on top of, the original picture instead of on a separate part of the page, seen in Alzheimer's or other visuospatial problems.

name: Cluster Breathing
formal: Irregular clusters of breaths with pauses; lower pontine / pontomedullary lesion in coma.
simple: An irregular breathing pattern with groups of breaths separated by pauses, seen with damage to the lower part of the brainstem in a critically ill or comatose patient.

name: Co-activation Sign
formal: Tremor amplitude increases with loading (organic tremor usually decreases); functional (psychogenic) tremor.
simple: A shaking tremor gets stronger, not weaker, when weight is added to the limb, the opposite of what happens with tremors caused by actual neurological disease; this suggests the tremor is non-organic (functional).

name: Cold Hands Sign
formal: Cold, dusky hands; multiple system atrophy (autonomic).
simple: Hands that are cold and bluish-purple in color, seen in a condition called multiple system atrophy that affects the body's automatic nervous system.

name: Collapsing Weakness
formal: Give-way weakness: full power briefly then sudden collapse; functional weakness or pain.
simple: When testing muscle strength, the limb feels strong for a moment then suddenly gives way, a pattern suggesting the weakness is non-organic (functional) or limited by pain, rather than true nerve or muscle damage.

name: Collier’s Sign
formal: Bilateral eyelid retraction ("posterior fossa stare"); dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome.
simple: Both upper eyelids are pulled up higher than normal, giving a staring appearance, from damage to a specific part of the midbrain.

name: Compulsive Grasping Hand
formal: Ongoing grasping of objects by one hand that must be restrained by the other; frontal/callosal lesions.
simple: One hand keeps grabbing onto nearby objects on its own, and the person may need to use their other hand to stop it, from damage to the front of the brain or the connection between brain hemispheres.

name: Conduite d’Approche
formal: Successive self-corrections homing in on a target word; conduction aphasia.
simple: A person repeatedly makes wrong attempts at a word, each one getting a little closer to the correct word until they finally say it right, seen in a language disorder called conduction aphasia.

name: Confabulation
formal: Production of false memories without intention to deceive; Korsakoff syndrome, frontal lesions.
simple: Making up false memories or stories without intending to lie, because the person genuinely believes what they are saying, classically in an alcohol-related memory disorder or frontal brain damage.

name: Confusion
formal: Inability to think with normal clarity and coherence; delirium, encephalopathy, attentional disorders.
simple: An inability to think clearly, stay oriented, or follow conversations normally, seen in delirium, brain dysfunction from illness, or attention problems.

name: Contracture
formal: Fixed shortening of muscle and tendon limiting joint movement.
simple: A permanent shortening and tightening of muscle and tendon that limits how far a joint can move.

name: Coprolalia
formal: Involuntary utterance of obscene words; Tourette syndrome.
simple: Involuntarily blurting out obscene or inappropriate words, a symptom seen in some people with Tourette syndrome.

name: Copropraxia
formal: Involuntary obscene gestures; Tourette syndrome.
simple: Involuntarily making obscene gestures, seen in some people with Tourette syndrome.

name: Corectopia
formal: Displaced, eccentric pupil; midbrain lesions or ocular causes.
simple: A pupil that sits off-center in an unusual position, either from a brain problem or from an issue within the eye itself.

name: Corneomandibular Reflex
formal: Corneal stimulation causes contralateral jaw deviation; bilateral UMN (supranuclear) lesions, coma.
simple: Touching the surface of the eye causes the jaw to jerk to the opposite side, an abnormal reflex seen with severe brain damage affecting both sides, or in unconscious patients.

name: Cortical Blindness
formal: Visual loss from bilateral occipital lesions with normal pupils and fundi; may be denied (Anton syndrome).
simple: Complete loss of vision even though the eyes themselves, including the pupils, look and react normally, because the problem lies in the vision-processing part of the brain rather than the eyes.

name: Cotard’s Syndrome
formal: Delusion of being dead or non-existent (nihilistic delusion); depression, psychosis, right hemisphere/frontal lesions.
simple: A false belief that one is dead, does not exist, or has lost internal organs, seen in severe depression, psychosis, or certain brain damage.

name: Cover Tests
formal: Cover–uncover and alternate cover tests to detect manifest (tropia) and latent (phoria) ocular deviation.
simple: Simple eye exam techniques where one eye is covered and then uncovered while watching how the eyes move, used to detect misalignment of the eyes that is either constant or only appears when one eye is covered.

name: Cramp
formal: Painful involuntary sustained muscle contraction relieved by stretching; motor neurone disease, neuropathy, metabolic causes, normal.
simple: A sudden, painful, involuntary tightening of a muscle that eases when the muscle is stretched, which can happen normally or with certain nerve or muscle diseases.

name: Cremasteric Reflex
formal: Stroking the inner thigh elevates the ipsilateral testis (L1–L2); lost in UMN lesions and L1–L2 root lesions.
simple: Stroking the inner thigh causes the testicle on that side to rise up, testing a specific level of nerves in the lower spinal cord; it is absent with damage to the brain's motor pathway or to those particular nerve roots.

name: Crocodile Tears
formal: Lacrimation when eating from aberrant regeneration after facial palsy.
simple: Tearing up while eating, caused by nerve fibers regrowing incorrectly after facial nerve damage and accidentally connecting to the tear glands instead of the salivary glands.

name: Curtaining
formal: Lifting a ptotic lid makes the other lid droop (Hering's law); myasthenia gravis.
simple: Lifting a droopy eyelid on one side makes the other eyelid droop instead, because the brain sends equal effort to both sides; seen in myasthenia gravis, a disease that weakens the muscles that lift the eyelids.

name: Cushing Reflex, Cushing Response
formal: Hypertension (wide pulse pressure), bradycardia and irregular breathing from rising ICP; impending herniation.
simple: A combination of high blood pressure, a slow heart rate, and irregular breathing that signals dangerously increased pressure inside the skull, a warning sign that the brain may be about to be pushed out of place.
aN: cushing reflex | cushing response

name: Dalrymple’s Sign
formal: Upper lid retraction exposing sclera above the cornea; thyroid eye disease.
simple: The upper eyelid sits too high, showing white of the eye above the colored part, seen in thyroid eye disease.

name: Dazzle
formal: Discomfort/visual impairment from bright light; cone dystrophy, optic neuropathy.
simple: Discomfort or worsened vision when exposed to bright light, seen in certain inherited eye conditions or optic nerve disease.

name: Decerebrate Rigidity
formal: Extensor posturing of arms and legs (arms extended, pronated); midbrain/upper pons lesions, poor prognosis in coma.
simple: Both arms and legs stiffly straighten out in an abnormal posture, a sign of severe damage to the middle or upper part of the brainstem, generally indicating a poor outlook in a comatose patient.

name: Decorticate Rigidity
formal: Flexion of the arms with extension of the legs; lesions above the red nucleus.
simple: The arms bend inward toward the chest while the legs straighten out, a posturing pattern from brain damage located above a certain deep brainstem structure.

name: Delirium
formal: Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with global cognitive impairment.
simple: A sudden, fluctuating state of confused thinking and poor attention along with widespread difficulty thinking clearly, usually caused by an underlying illness, infection, or medication.

name: Dementia
formal: Acquired decline in multiple cognitive domains sufficient to impair daily function.
simple: A gradually acquired decline across several areas of thinking ability (like memory, language, and judgment) that is severe enough to interfere with daily life.

name: Depersonalisation
formal: Feeling detached from one's self or body, as if an observer; dissociation, anxiety, epilepsy.
simple: A feeling of being detached from oneself, as though watching one's own body and thoughts from the outside, seen with anxiety, stress-related conditions, or occasionally epilepsy.

name: Derealisation
formal: Feeling that the surroundings are unreal; dissociation, anxiety, temporal lobe epilepsy.
simple: A feeling that the surrounding world is unreal, dreamlike, or distant, seen with anxiety, stress-related conditions, or certain seizures.

name: Dermatomal Sensory Loss
formal: Sensory loss confined to one dermatome, localising to a single nerve root or spinal segment.
simple: Numbness limited to a specific band of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve, which helps pinpoint the exact spinal nerve root or segment that is affected.

name: Dermo-Optical Perception
formal: Claimed ability to perceive colours/print by touch ("fingertip sight") — of doubtful validity.
simple: A claimed but scientifically unproven ability to sense colors or read print through the fingertips without seeing them.

name: Diagonistic Dyspraxia
formal: One hand acts in opposition to the other (e.g. undoing buttons the other hand does up); callosal lesions.
simple: One hand starts doing the opposite of what the other hand is doing, such as undoing a button the other hand just did up, seen with damage to the connection between the two halves of the brain.

name: Diamond on Quadriceps Sign
formal: Diamond-shaped bulge of the quadriceps with the knee slightly bent; dysferlinopathy (LGMD2B/Miyoshi).
simple: A diamond-shaped bulge appears in the thigh muscle when the knee is slightly bent, a finding in a specific inherited muscle-wasting disease.

name: Diaphragm Weakness
formal: Orthopnoea, paradoxical abdominal movement, fall in vital capacity supine; C3–5 cord, phrenic nerve, MND, acid maltase deficiency, MG.
simple: Weakness of the main breathing muscle causing breathlessness worse lying flat, an unusual inward belly movement with each breath, and reduced breathing capacity; causes include certain spine, nerve, or muscle diseases.

name: Diplophonia
formal: Voice with two simultaneous pitches from vocal cord asymmetry (e.g. unilateral cord paralysis).
simple: The voice sounds like it is producing two pitches at once, because the two vocal cords are vibrating unevenly, often from paralysis of one vocal cord.

name: Diplopia
formal: Double vision; binocular (ocular misalignment) vs monocular (ocular causes).
simple: Double vision, which can occur because the two eyes are not aligned properly (seen with both eyes open) or, less commonly, from a problem within a single eye (still present with one eye closed).

name: Directional Hypokinesia
formal: Slowness/reluctance to move toward contralesional space; neglect syndrome.
simple: A slowness or reluctance to move toward one particular side of space, even when strength is normal, seen in one-sided neglect after a stroke.

name: Disc Swelling
formal: Swollen optic disc: papilledema (raised ICP) vs optic neuritis, ischemic optic neuropathy, infiltration.
simple: Swelling of the optic disc at the back of the eye, which can be caused by raised pressure inside the skull, or by inflammation, poor blood supply, or infiltration of the optic nerve itself.

name: Dissociated Sensory Loss
formal: Loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch/proprioception (or vice versa); syringomyelia, anterior spinal artery syndrome, small-fibre neuropathy.
simple: A pattern where pain and temperature sensation are lost while touch and position sense are preserved, or the reverse, pointing to specific spinal cord or nerve damage.

name: Dissociation
formal: Pupils react better to near than to light; Argyll Robertson, Adie, dorsal midbrain lesions, optic neuropathy.
simple: The pupils respond better when focusing on something close than they do to bright light, an unusual pattern seen in certain pupil disorders, midbrain lesions, or optic nerve disease.

name: Divisional Palsy
formal: Selective palsy of the superior or inferior division of the III nerve; lesion in cavernous sinus / orbit.
simple: Only part of the eye-movement nerve (the third cranial nerve) is affected, weakening either the upper or lower group of eye muscles it controls, usually from a lesion near the eye socket or the base of the skull.

name: Doll’s Eye Manoeuvre, Doll’s Head Manoeuvre
formal: Oculocephalic reflex: eyes move opposite to passive head rotation when brainstem intact (in coma).
simple: When the head is turned side to side in an unconscious patient, the eyes move in the opposite direction as if still looking at the same spot, showing that the brainstem controlling eye movement is still working.
nN: doll eye maneuvre doll head maneuvre
aN: doll eye maneuvre | doll head maneuvre

name: Double Elevator Palsy
formal: Weak elevation of one eye in both abduction and adduction; supranuclear (pretectal) or congenital.
simple: One eye cannot look upward properly no matter which direction it is turned, from a problem either in the brain's eye-movement control center or present from birth.

name: Drusen
formal: Hyaline bodies of the optic disc (pseudopapilloedema) or retina (macular drusen).
simple: Small yellowish deposits that build up in the eye, either on the optic nerve (which can look like swelling but is not) or in the retina (linked to age-related eye disease).

name: Durkan’s Compression Test
formal: Direct pressure over the carpal tunnel for 30 s reproduces median paraesthesia; carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: Pressing directly over the front of the wrist for about 30 seconds brings on tingling in the thumb-side fingers, a test used to help diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome (a pinched wrist nerve).

name: Dynamic Aphasia
formal: Marked reduction in spontaneous speech with preserved naming, repetition and comprehension; frontal lesions.
simple: The person talks much less than normal on their own, but can still name things, repeat words, and understand speech fine. It points to damage in the front part of the brain.

name: Dysaesthesia
formal: Unpleasant abnormal sensation, spontaneous or evoked.
simple: An unpleasant, abnormal feeling on the skin, like burning or crawling, that happens either on its own or when touched.

name: Dysautonomia
formal: Autonomic dysfunction: orthostatic hypotension, sweating, bladder, bowel, sexual and pupillary abnormalities.
simple: The automatic nervous system that controls things like blood pressure, sweating, bladder, and pupils stops working properly.

name: Dysexecutive Syndrome
formal: Impaired planning, organisation, set-shifting and judgment; frontal–subcortical dysfunction.
simple: Trouble planning, organizing, switching between tasks, and making good decisions, caused by problems in the brain's frontal areas.

name: Dysgeusia
formal: Distorted taste.
simple: Taste that is distorted or abnormal.

name: Dyskinesia
formal: General term for involuntary movements; commonly levodopa-induced or tardive dyskinesia.
simple: A general term for unwanted, uncontrollable movements, often caused by long-term Parkinson's medication or antipsychotic drugs.

name: Dyslexia
formal: Difficulty reading — developmental or acquired (alexia).
simple: Trouble reading, either present from childhood or caused later by a brain injury.

name: Dysmentia
formal: Term proposed instead of "dementia" to emphasise potentially treatable/preventable cognitive decline.
simple: A suggested replacement for the word "dementia" to highlight that some memory and thinking decline can be treated or prevented.

name: Dysmorphopsia
formal: Distortion of the shape of seen objects; macular or cortical lesions.
simple: Objects look the wrong shape, caused by problems in the eye's retina or the brain's visual areas.

name: Dysphonia
formal: Impaired voice production (hoarse, breathy); laryngeal dystonia (spasmodic dysphonia), vocal cord palsy.
simple: A change in voice quality, like hoarseness or breathiness, from problems in the voice box, including a spasming voice (spasmodic dysphonia) or a paralyzed vocal cord.

name: Dyspraxia
formal: Impaired skilled movements not explained by weakness or sensory loss; apraxia.
simple: Difficulty performing skilled, coordinated movements that isn't caused by weakness or numbness.

name: Dystextia
formal: Disordered mobile phone text messages as a presentation of aphasia (e.g. acute stroke).
simple: Odd, garbled text messages that reveal a language problem, sometimes an early sign of stroke.

name: Dystypia
formal: Selective impairment of typing without aphasia/apraxia; left frontal lesions.
simple: Trouble typing specifically, even though speaking and other skilled movements are normal; linked to damage on the brain's left front side.

name: Eastchester Clapping Sign
formal: Asked to clap, a hemiplegic patient with neglect moves the good hand only to the midline (does not reach across); sign of neglect.
simple: When asked to clap, a patient with one-sided paralysis and inattention to that side only brings the good hand to the middle instead of clapping both hands together; a sign of neglecting one side of the body.

name: Echolalia
formal: Automatic repetition of the examiner's words; transcortical aphasia, frontal lesions, autism, Tourette.
simple: Automatically repeating back words the examiner just said, seen in certain language disorders, frontal brain damage, autism, or Tourette syndrome.

name: Echolocation
formal: Using echoes (e.g. tongue clicks) to perceive surroundings; learned by some blind people.
simple: Using sound echoes, such as tongue clicks, to sense one's surroundings, a skill some blind people learn.

name: Echophenomena
formal: Automatic imitation of others' words (echolalia) or actions (echopraxia); frontal lesions, Tourette, catatonia.
simple: Automatically copying other people's words or actions, seen with frontal brain damage, Tourette syndrome, or catatonia.

name: Echopraxia
formal: Automatic imitation of the examiner's actions; frontal lesions, Tourette, catatonia.
simple: Automatically copying the examiner's actions or gestures, seen with frontal brain damage, Tourette syndrome, or catatonia.

name: Eidetic Memory
formal: Unusually vivid, detailed visual memory ("photographic").
simple: An unusually vivid and detailed visual memory, sometimes called "photographic memory."

name: Eight-And-A-Half Syndrome
formal: One-and-a-half syndrome plus ipsilateral facial (VII) palsy; dorsal pontine tegmental lesion.
simple: A combination of two specific eye-movement problems plus weakness of one side of the face, caused by a lesion deep in the brainstem.

name: Ekbom’s Syndrome
formal: Delusional parasitosis — fixed belief of skin infestation with insects (not restless legs).
simple: A false, fixed belief that insects are infesting the skin, despite no evidence; different from restless legs syndrome.

name: Emprosthotonos
formal: Flexion posture of head on trunk and trunk on knees (opposite of opisthotonos); tetanus or "bowing" seizures.
simple: A body posture where the head bends forward onto the chest and the trunk bends forward onto the knees, seen in tetanus or certain seizures.

name: Encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction with altered consciousness/cognition (metabolic, toxic, infective).
simple: Widespread brain dysfunction causing confusion or altered consciousness, from causes like metabolic problems, toxins, or infection.

name: Enophthalmos
formal: Posterior displacement of the globe; orbital floor fracture, (apparent) in Horner syndrome.
simple: The eyeball sits abnormally deep in its socket, from an orbital bone fracture or, apparently, in some cases of Horner syndrome.

name: Entomopia
formal: Multiple images like an insect eye (polyopia).
simple: Seeing many repeated copies of an image, like an insect's compound eye.

name: Entrainment Test
formal: Tremor adopts the frequency of voluntary rhythmic tapping by another limb — suggests functional tremor.
simple: A hand tremor changes its speed to match a rhythmic tapping movement done by the other hand, suggesting the tremor is not from a physical brain disease but psychological in origin.

name: Environmental Tilt
formal: Perception that the environment is tilted or upside down; brainstem/vestibular or parietal lesions.
simple: Feeling that the surroundings are tilted or upside down, from a problem in the brainstem, balance system, or a brain region called the parietal lobe.

name: Epiphora
formal: Overflow of tears; facial palsy with ectropion, lacrimal obstruction.
simple: Tears overflow and run down the face, from facial nerve weakness with eyelid turning outward, or a blocked tear duct.

name: Erythropsia
formal: Objects appear tinged red; after cataract surgery, drugs, cortical lesions.
simple: Everything looks tinged red, which can happen after cataract surgery, from certain drugs, or brain lesions.

name: Esophoria
formal: Latent inward deviation of an eye, revealed by cover test.
simple: A tendency for one eye to drift inward, only revealed when a special eye-covering test is done.

name: Esotropia
formal: Manifest inward deviation of an eye (convergent squint).
simple: One eye is visibly and constantly turned inward (a type of crossed eyes).

name: Ewart Phenomenon
formal: Ptotic lid rises with each swallow — a synkinesis due to misdirected nerve regrowth.
simple: A drooping eyelid lifts up when swallowing, caused by nerve fibers regrowing to the wrong muscle.

name: Exophoria
formal: Latent outward deviation of an eye, revealed by cover test.
simple: A tendency for one eye to drift outward, only revealed when a special eye-covering test is done.

name: Exophthalmos
formal: Forward protrusion of the globe; thyroid eye disease, orbital mass (see proptosis).
simple: The eyeball bulges forward out of its socket, seen in thyroid eye disease or a mass behind the eye.

name: Exosomaesthesia
formal: Referring a tactile stimulus to a point outside the body; parietal lobe lesions.
simple: Feeling a touch on the skin as if it were happening outside the body, from damage to the parietal lobe of the brain.

name: Exotropia
formal: Manifest outward deviation of an eye (divergent squint).
simple: One eye is visibly and constantly turned outward (a type of crossed eyes).

name: Extinction
formal: Failure to perceive a stimulus on one side when both sides are stimulated simultaneously, though perceived alone; parietal lesions.
simple: When touched or shown something on both sides of the body at once, the patient only notices one side, even though they can feel each side fine on its own; from parietal lobe damage.

name: Facilitation
formal: Increase in strength or reflexes after brief exercise; Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
simple: Muscle strength or reflexes temporarily get stronger right after brief exercise, seen in a nerve-muscle disorder called Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

name: False-Localising Signs
formal: Signs pointing to a site distant from the lesion, e.g. VI nerve palsy from raised ICP, Kernohan notch.
simple: Neurological signs that seem to point to the wrong location, because they actually come from pressure effects elsewhere in the brain, such as raised pressure inside the skull.

name: Femoral Nerve Stretch Test
formal: Prone knee flexion/hip extension reproduces anterior thigh pain; upper lumbar (L2–L4) root irritation.
simple: Bending the knee while the patient lies face down and extending the hip brings on pain down the front of the thigh, suggesting a pinched nerve root in the upper lower back.

name: Fencer’s Posture, Fencing Posture
formal: Head turned to one side with the arm extended on that side and flexed on the other; supplementary motor area seizures.
simple: During a seizure, the head turns to one side while that arm straightens out and the other arm bends, like a fencer's stance; comes from a specific brain seizure area.
aN: fencer posture | fencing posture

name: Festinant Gait, Festination
formal: Short, progressively faster steps as if chasing the center of gravity; Parkinson's disease.
simple: Small, quick, speeding-up steps as if chasing one's own center of gravity, typical of Parkinson's disease.
aN: festinant gait | festination

name: Fibrillation
formal: Spontaneous single muscle fibre discharges seen on EMG (not visible clinically except in the tongue); denervation.
simple: Tiny, spontaneous twitches of single muscle fibers, usually only detectable with a needle test (not visible to the eye, except sometimes in the tongue); a sign nerves supplying the muscle are damaged.

name: Finger Agnosia
formal: Inability to name or identify one's own/others' fingers; dominant parietal, Gerstmann syndrome.
simple: Trouble naming or identifying one's own or someone else's fingers, seen with damage to a specific area of the brain's left side.

name: Finger-Floor Distance
formal: Fingertip-to-floor distance on forward bending; >25 cm supports lumbosacral root compression in sciatica.
simple: How far the fingertips are from the floor when bending forward; a large distance supports a pinched nerve in the lower back causing sciatica.

name: Fisher’s Sign
formal: Paucity of emotional facial expression (emotional facial paresis) with preserved voluntary movement; non-dominant (right) hemisphere lesions.
simple: Reduced emotional facial expression while voluntary facial movements stay normal, seen with damage to the right side of the brain.

name: Flail Limb
formal: Severe proximal-predominant symmetric arm weakness and wasting with relatively spared legs; ALS variant (brachial amyotrophic diplegia).
simple: Severe weakness and muscle wasting mainly in the shoulders and arms, with the legs relatively spared; a form of motor neuron disease.

name: Flexion-Adduction Sign
formal: Patient holds the painful arm bent at the elbow and pulled into the side to protect it; seen in neuralgic amyotrophy.
simple: Holding the arm bent at the elbow and pulled in against the body to avoid pain, seen in a painful nerve condition affecting the shoulder and arm.

name: Flick Sign
formal: Shaking or flicking the hand relieves nocturnal paresthesia; carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: Shaking or flicking the hand relieves nighttime tingling or numbness, a symptom of carpal tunnel syndrome (a pinched wrist nerve).

name: Flynn Phenomenon
formal: Paradoxical pupil constriction in darkness; congenital retinal disorders.
simple: The pupil paradoxically gets smaller in the dark instead of bigger, seen in some inherited eye disorders present from birth.

name: Fonzarelli Sign
formal: Involuntary "thumbs up" thumb extension — focal thumb dystonia in parkinsonism.
simple: An involuntary "thumbs up" movement from muscle spasm limited to the thumb, seen in Parkinson's disease.

name: Foot Drop
formal: Weak ankle dorsiflexion; L5 root, common peroneal nerve, sciatic nerve, motor neurone disease or central causes.
simple: Weakness lifting the foot upward at the ankle, from a pinched nerve in the lower back or leg, or from brain or spinal cord disease.

name: Forced Ductions
formal: Passive movement of the anesthetised globe with forceps to detect mechanical restriction (e.g. thyroid eye disease, orbital fracture).
simple: The eye doctor numbs the eye and physically moves it with forceps to check if something is mechanically blocking its movement, such as in thyroid eye disease or an eye socket fracture.

name: Forced Groping
formal: Hand follows and gropes toward visual/tactile stimuli; frontal lesions.
simple: The hand automatically reaches out and grasps at things it sees or touches, without the person meaning to; from frontal brain damage.

name: Forearm and Finger Rolling
formal: Rolling forearms/index fingers around each other: the weak (UMN) side stays relatively still while the other orbits it; subtle corticospinal lesion.
simple: Asking the patient to roll their forearms or index fingers around each other: the side with subtle nerve damage barely moves while the normal side does the work, revealing a mild weakness that's otherwise hard to detect.

name: Foreign Accent Syndrome
formal: Speech sounds as if spoken with a foreign accent; left frontal/basal ganglia lesions, or functional.
simple: Someone's speech suddenly sounds like it has a foreign accent, from a brain lesion or, sometimes, a psychological cause.

name: Formication
formal: Sensation of insects crawling on or under the skin; neuropathy, drugs (cocaine), delusional parasitosis.
simple: A crawling, itching sensation as if insects were on or under the skin; seen with nerve damage, certain drugs like cocaine, or a false belief in skin infestation.

name: Fortification Spectra
formal: Scintillating zigzag lines of migraine visual aura (teichopsia).
simple: Shimmering, zigzag patterns of light seen during a migraine's visual warning phase (aura).

name: Foster Kennedy Syndrome
formal: Ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema; frontal (olfactory groove) tumor.
simple: One optic nerve is shrunken and damaged while the other eye shows swelling from pressure, caused by a tumor at the front of the brain.

name: Fou Rire Prodromique
formal: Uncontrollable laughter heralding stroke, usually basilar artery/pontine.
simple: Sudden uncontrollable laughing that occurs right before a stroke, usually one affecting the back part of the brain.

name: Freezing of Gait
formal: Sudden brief inability to initiate or continue walking ("feet glued to the floor"); PD, vascular parkinsonism.
simple: Suddenly and briefly being unable to start or keep walking, as if the feet are stuck to the floor; seen in Parkinson's disease and related conditions.

name: Froment’s Sign
formal: Flexion of the thumb IP joint (FPL, median) when holding paper between thumb and index, compensating for weak adductor pollicis; ulnar neuropathy.
simple: When asked to pinch paper between thumb and index finger, the thumb tip bends instead of staying straight, because a hand nerve (the ulnar nerve) is damaged and a backup muscle is compensating.
th: หนีบกระดาษระหว่างนิ้วโป้งกับนิ้วชี้แล้วนิ้วโป้งงอ — กล้ามเนื้อ adductor pollicis อ่อนแรง (เส้นประสาท ulnar)
exam: Ask the patient to hold a piece of paper pinched between the thumb and the radial side of the index finger while you try to pull it out.
pos: Thumb IP flexion (FPL substituting for adductor pollicis) = ulnar nerve palsy.
aN: froment | paper sign

det.mechanism: A key pinch, holding a flat object between the straight thumb and the side of the index finger, is powered mainly by adductor pollicis and the first dorsal interosseous, both supplied by the ulnar nerve through its deep palmar motor branch. When these muscles are weak, the patient keeps hold by recruiting flexor pollicis longus, which the median nerve innervates via its anterior interosseous branch. Flexor pollicis longus bends the thumb's interphalangeal joint, so the thumb tip curls onto the paper instead of lying flat against it. The sign is therefore a visible trick movement substituting median for ulnar function.
det.technique: Give the patient a sheet of paper or card to hold in each hand between the extended thumb and the radial side of the index finger, then pull both sheets away at the same time and compare. A positive sign is flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint on the affected side as the patient resists; the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint may hyperextend at the same time (Jeanne sign). Make sure the patient does not simply pinch with the fingertips, and test both sides so subtle asymmetry is seen. Then examine first dorsal interosseous, abductor digiti minimi and finger abduction directly.
det.interpretation: A positive sign means weakness of ulnar-innervated intrinsic hand muscles but does not show where the lesion is. Possible sites include ulnar compression around the elbow (the commonest), at Guyon's canal or in the palm, the plexus lower trunk or medial cord (for example neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome or Pancoast tumour), the C8–T1 roots, or the anterior horn cells, as in ALS with its 'split hand'. Sensory loss over the dorsal ulnar hand points proximal to the wrist, sparing of sensation suggests a deep palmar branch lesion or motor neuron disease, and medial forearm sensory loss suggests plexus or root disease. Nerve conduction studies and EMG define the site and severity. When the ulnar nerve is injured at the elbow, the first dorsal interosseous is the muscle most often weak (in over 80% of cases), ahead of abductor digiti minimi, whereas the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus and especially flexor carpi ulnaris are frequently spared, so a positive Froment sign with normal forearm muscles does not place the lesion at the wrist.
pearls: Thumb IP flexion during key pinch = FPL substituting for weak adductor pollicis.
Froment sign with a strong FCU can still be an elbow lesion — FCU is often spared by fascicular selectivity.
Pair with Wartenberg sign (abducted little finger) and first dorsal interosseous testing.
Dorsal hand sensation spared with intrinsic weakness: think Guyon's canal deep branch or motor neuron disease.
Needs an intact anterior interosseous nerve — in a combined median-ulnar lesion the trick may not appear.
det.thd: Froment sign คือเมื่อให้หนีบกระดาษระหว่างนิ้วโป้งที่เหยียดตรงกับข้างนิ้วชี้แล้วดึงออก ผู้ป่วยต้องงอข้อปลายนิ้วโป้งโดยใช้ FPL (เส้นประสาท median สาขา anterior interosseous) แทน adductor pollicis และ first dorsal interosseous ที่อ่อนแรงจากเส้นประสาท ulnar ให้ตรวจสองมือพร้อมกันเพื่อเทียบ และอาจพบข้อ MCP นิ้วโป้งแอ่นร่วม (Jeanne sign) ผลบวกบ่งชี้กล้ามเนื้อมือที่เลี้ยงด้วย ulnar อ่อนแรง ซึ่งอาจเกิดจากรอยโรคที่ข้อศอก Guyon's canal, lower trunk ของ brachial plexus, ราก C8–T1 หรือ ALS จึงต้องใช้การตรวจความรู้สึกและ NCS/EMG ช่วยหาตำแหน่ง

name: Frontal Lobe Syndromes
formal: Dorsolateral (dysexecutive), orbitofrontal (disinhibited) and medial (apathetic) frontal syndromes.
simple: Different patterns of personality and behavior change depending on which part of the brain's frontal lobe is damaged: poor planning, loss of social restraint, or lack of motivation.

name: Fugue
formal: Episode of wandering with amnesia; dissociative or post-ictal.
simple: A period of wandering combined with memory loss for that time, seen after a seizure or during severe psychological stress.

name: Functional Weakness and Sensory Disturbance
formal: Deficits inconsistent with neuroanatomy (Hoover sign, give-way weakness, midline splitting of sensation).
simple: Weakness or numbness that doesn't match how the nervous system is actually wired, suggesting the cause is not structural brain or nerve damage but a functional (mind-body) disorder.

name: Funnel Vision
formal: Severe constriction of the visual field; glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa, functional (non-expanding with distance).
simple: Severe narrowing of what a person can see around the edges, from eye disease like glaucoma, or sometimes from a non-physical cause.

name: Gait Apraxia
formal: Difficulty initiating and sustaining walking with preserved leg movements in bed; frontal lesions, NPH (magnetic gait).
simple: Trouble starting and continuing to walk, even though leg movements are normal while lying in bed; seen with frontal brain damage or a condition where fluid builds up in the brain.

name: Gambling
formal: Pathological gambling — impulse control disorder with dopamine agonists in Parkinson's disease.
simple: Compulsive, uncontrollable gambling, a known side effect of certain Parkinson's disease medications.

name: Ganser Phenomenon, Ganser Syndrome
formal: Approximate answers to simple questions (vorbeireden); dissociative states.
simple: Giving answers to simple questions that are close but clearly wrong, seen in some psychological conditions.
aN: ganser phenomenon | ganser syndrome

name: Gaping
formal: Involuntary mouth opening — focal jaw-opening dystonia (Brueghel syndrome).
simple: Uncontrollable opening of the mouth from muscle spasms affecting the jaw.

name: Gaslight Phenomenon, Gaslight Syndrome
formal: One person attempts to make another believe they are mentally ill; must be recognised in cognitive/psychiatric assessment.
simple: When someone tries to convince another person they are losing their mind; doctors need to recognize this when assessing a patient's mental state.
aN: gaslight phenomenon | gaslight syndrome

name: Gaze-Evoked Phenomena
formal: Symptoms or movements triggered by eccentric gaze (gaze-evoked nystagmus, amaurosis, tinnitus).
simple: Symptoms like jerking eye movements, temporary blindness, or ringing in the ears that appear only when looking in a particular direction.

name: Gerstmann Syndrome
formal: Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and right–left disorientation; dominant angular gyrus.
simple: A group of problems occurring together: trouble writing, trouble with math, trouble identifying fingers, and confusing left and right; from damage to a specific brain area.

name: Geschwind Syndrome
formal: Interictal personality change in temporal lobe epilepsy: hypergraphia, hyperreligiosity, hyposexuality.
simple: A cluster of personality traits sometimes seen between seizures in people with temporal lobe epilepsy: excessive writing, intense religious interest, and reduced sexual interest.

name: Gibbus
formal: Sharply angled kyphosis from vertebral collapse (e.g. tuberculosis).
simple: A sharp, angled hump in the spine caused by a collapsed vertebra, for example from tuberculosis.

name: Girdle Sensation
formal: Band-like tightness around the trunk; spinal cord (dorsal column/root) lesions, MS.
simple: A tight, band-like feeling wrapped around the body, from a spinal cord problem such as multiple sclerosis.

name: Glove And Stocking Sensory Loss
formal: Distal symmetric sensory loss in hands and feet; length-dependent polyneuropathy.
simple: Numbness affecting the hands and feet in a pattern like gloves and socks, from nerve damage that worsens the farther it is from the body's core.

name: Gordon’s Sign
formal: Squeezing the calf muscles produces an extensor plantar response; corticospinal tract lesion.
simple: Squeezing the calf muscle makes the big toe point upward, an abnormal reflex indicating damage to the brain's or spinal cord's movement pathways.
