name: Linear Radial Perivascular Enhancement (GFAP Astrocytopathy)
formal: Post-gadolinium T1 MRI pattern of thin linear enhancing streaks running outward from the lateral ventricles through the white matter, perpendicular to the ventricular wall and following perivascular spaces; seen in about half of people with autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy and suggestive of the disease when combined with a compatible meningoencephalomyelitis.
simple: On a contrast MRI, thin bright lines fan out from the fluid spaces in the middle of the brain like the spokes of a wheel. It is a clue to an autoimmune brain inflammation called GFAP astrocytopathy.
ab: perivascular radiating enhancement from the ventricles
th: ภาพ MRI หลังฉีดสารทึบแสงเห็นเส้นตรงบาง ๆ enhance พุ่งออกจากผนัง ventricle เข้าสู่เนื้อสมองขาวตามช่องว่างรอบหลอดเลือด พบประมาณครึ่งหนึ่งของผู้ป่วย autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy ช่วยชี้นำเมื่อมีอาการ meningoencephalomyelitis
exam: Not a bedside sign: order contrast-enhanced T1 MRI in any subacute meningoencephalitis with fever, headache, tremor, urinary retention or myelitis, and look at axial slices for lines perpendicular to the ventricles. Also inspect the spinal cord and leptomeninges, and send CSF GFAP-IgG by cell-based assay.
pos: Linear radial perivascular enhancement raises the probability of autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy and justifies CSF antibody testing and early immunotherapy once infection is reasonably excluded. It is absent in around half of antibody-positive patients, including some with normal brain MRI, so a negative scan does not exclude the disease. Similar linear enhancement has been reported in neurosarcoidosis, CLIPPERS and lymphoma.

det.technique: Obtain axial and coronal post-contrast T1 images with fat suppression or 3D sequences and scroll for fine lines fanning out from the lateral ventricles; also check the leptomeninges, brainstem, optic nerves and the whole spinal cord. Pair the scan with CSF cell count, protein, glucose and GFAP-IgG.
det.interpretation: The pattern appears in roughly half of cases and increases suspicion in a meningoencephalitis that does not respond to antimicrobials. It is not exclusive to GFAP astrocytopathy, since sarcoidosis, CLIPPERS and lymphoma can appear similar, and some people show only leptomeningeal or splenial changes or none.
pearls: Fever, tremor and urinary retention plus radial enhancement: send CSF GFAP-IgG.
A normal brain MRI does not rule out GFAP astrocytopathy; look at the spine.
Tuberculous meningitis is the main mimic in Thailand, so test for TB in parallel before steroids.

name: Raised CSF Interleukin-6 (Neuro-Behçet Disease)
formal: Persistent elevation of interleukin-6 in cerebrospinal fluid, using a Japanese cut-off of roughly 17 pg/mL, measured after acute treatment has settled, which separates chronic progressive neuro-Behçet disease from the recovery phase of an acute attack and is used to monitor response to methotrexate or infliximab.
simple: A raised level of an inflammatory chemical (IL-6) in the spinal fluid of a Behçet patient whose brain disease is slowly progressing. It shows that the brain inflammation is still smouldering even when the person looks quiet.
th: ระดับ interleukin-6 ใน CSF ที่สูง (ประมาณมากกว่า 17 pg/mL ตามเกณฑ์ญี่ปุ่น) ในผู้ป่วย Behçet ที่เคยมีอาการกำเริบเฉียบพลัน ใช้แยก chronic progressive neuro-Behçet ออกจากระยะฟื้นตัวของ acute attack และใช้ติดตามผลการรักษา
exam: Not a bedside sign: when acute neuro-Behçet disease has improved and the steroid dose is below about 10 mg/day, request CSF IL-6; if it is above the threshold, repeat after at least two weeks. High-dose steroids can transiently lower the value and give a false negative, so avoid sampling during large doses.
pos: Two consecutive high values, or one high value with brainstem atrophy on MRI, support chronic progressive neuro-Behçet disease and a change of treatment toward methotrexate and then infliximab. In a Japanese series a cut-off of 17 pg/mL gave sensitivity about 92% and specificity about 95% for separating chronic progressive from convalescent acute disease. The assay is not widely available and the cut-off is local, so interpret with MRI and clinical course; other brain inflammation may also raise IL-6.

CSF levels therefore track the smouldering parenchymal process better than cell counts.
det.technique: Take CSF when the acute attack has subsided and prednisolone is below about 10 mg/day, because larger doses may suppress IL-6 temporarily. If the first value is high, repeat after two weeks or more; during stable treatment repeat every 6 to 12 months.
det.interpretation: A persistently raised level, together with brainstem atrophy, supports chronic progressive disease, whereas normalisation suggests the recovery stage of an acute attack. The 17 pg/mL cut-off comes from Japanese series and should be validated locally. IL-6 also rises in other CNS inflammation and infection, so combine it with MRI and clinical course.
pearls: Sample after the steroid dose has fallen, not in the middle of pulse treatment.
Brainstem atrophy with high CSF IL-6 favours chronic progressive neuro-Behçet over spinocerebellar degeneration.
Goal of treatment: IL-6 down, no clinical progression, no further brainstem atrophy.

name: Storiform Fibrosis with Obliterative Phlebitis (IgG4-RD)
formal: Histopathological pair of findings in IgG4-related disease: dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate arranged in a spiralling cartwheel pattern of fibrosis (storiform fibrosis) together with inflammation and occlusion of veins (obliterative phlebitis); recognised by the 2020 Japanese revised comprehensive criteria as diagnostic even when IgG4 immunostaining is poor.
simple: Under the microscope the scar tissue swirls in a cartwheel pattern and small veins are blocked by inflammation. Together with many IgG4-producing plasma cells, this pattern identifies IgG4-related disease in a biopsy of dura, orbit, pituitary or other organ.
th: ลักษณะทางพยาธิวิทยาของ IgG4-RD คือ fibrosis แบบวนคล้ายล้อเกวียน (storiform fibrosis) ร่วมกับการอักเสบและอุดตันของหลอดเลือดดำ (obliterative phlebitis) และมี lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate เกณฑ์ปี 2020 ของญี่ปุ่นยอมรับลักษณะนี้จาก H&E แม้การย้อม IgG4 ไม่ชัด
exam: Not a bedside sign: biopsy the most accessible lesion (dura, lacrimal gland, orbital mass, pituitary or salivary gland) and ask the pathologist to report storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis and IgG4-positive plasma cells with the IgG4/IgG ratio. Request elastin staining for veins and repeat staining when background is high.
pos: Storiform fibrosis with obliterative phlebitis, plus lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, strongly supports IgG4-RD, which is helpful because serum IgG4 has limited sensitivity and specificity. The infiltrate must be assessed with clinical and radiological features because IgG4-positive cells also occur in lymphoma, cancers, ANCA vasculitis and other inflammatory conditions. Biopsy of the pancreas, retroperitoneum or ocular cavity can be difficult.

det.mechanism: IgG4-RD is a fibroinflammatory disorder in which T follicular helper cells and B cells drive plasmablast expansion and release profibrotic cytokines, so myofibroblasts lay down collagen in a swirling arrangement. Veins are targeted by the infiltrate, and their lumina are narrowed or obliterated.
det.technique: Biopsy the safest accessible lesion and give the pathologist the clinical question. Ask for H&E assessment, IgG and IgG4 immunostains with counts per high-power field, an IgG4/IgG ratio, and elastic staining to show the vein walls. Sampling error is common in fibrotic or small specimens.
det.interpretation: The 2020 Japanese revised criteria treat the combination of lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with storiform fibrosis or obliterative phlebitis as a pathological hallmark, useful when staining is unclear. The result must be viewed with imaging and serum IgG4, since IgG4-positive plasma cells also accumulate in lymphoma, ANCA vasculitis, malignancy and other disorders.
pearls: No single feature proves IgG4-RD: put histology, serum IgG4 (cut-off 135 mg/dL) and imaging together.
Normal serum IgG4 does not exclude the disease; biopsy decides.
Always exclude lymphoma and ANCA vasculitis in a dural or orbital biopsy that shows IgG4 cells.

name: Claustrum Sign
formal: Bilateral or asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, sometimes with swelling and restricted diffusion, of the claustrum, the thin grey-matter lamina between the external and extreme capsules; described in febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome as well as other cytokine-mediated encephalopathies.
simple: On a brain MRI, a thin bright ribbon appears beside the insula where the claustrum lies. It suggests that inflammation driven by cytokines is affecting the brain, as in some cases of severe seizures after a fever.
th: สัญญาณ T2/FLAIR สูงที่ claustrum ซึ่งเป็นแผ่นเนื้อเทาบางๆ ระหว่าง external capsule และ extreme capsule พบใน FIRES และโรคสมองจากพายุไซโตไคน์อื่นๆ เช่น acute necrotising encephalopathy, COVID-19 encephalopathy และ ICANS
exam: Not a bedside sign: review thin-slice axial and coronal FLAIR and T2 images for a linear bright strip lateral to the external capsule and medial to the insular cortex, and check diffusion-weighted images for restricted diffusion. Look also at the pulvinar and hippocampus, which are often involved, and scan again after several weeks because signal may fade or progress to atrophy.
pos: A hyperintense claustrum in a patient with new-onset refractory status epilepticus after a febrile illness supports FIRES and a cytokine-driven mechanism, although the sign is not specific and may follow prolonged seizures. It should prompt a search for treatable autoimmune, infectious and genetic causes and a discussion of early immunotherapy. Absence of the sign does not exclude FIRES.

det.mechanism: The claustrum is a narrow layer of grey matter with dense connections to widespread cortical areas and a high density of receptors for inflammatory mediators. In cytokine-driven encephalopathies, interleukin and interferon signalling may cause vasogenic and cytotoxic oedema there before other regions are visibly affected. Prolonged seizures can also produce signal change, so the sign marks neuroinflammation or sustained excitation.
det.technique: Review thin-slice axial and coronal FLAIR and T2 images with attention to the strip between the external and extreme capsules, and add diffusion-weighted images. Repeat MRI after a few weeks to see whether signal resolves or atrophy follows.
det.interpretation: The sign has been reported in febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome, acute necrotising encephalopathy, COVID-19-related encephalopathy and CAR-T neurotoxicity, supporting a shared cytokine pathway. It is supportive rather than diagnostic, and a normal claustrum does not exclude any of these disorders.
pearls: New-onset refractory seizures after a fever + hyperintense claustrum = think FIRES.
Also look at the pulvinar and hippocampus.

name: Inverted Knee Jerk (Inverted Patellar Reflex)
formal: Paradoxical response to tapping the patellar tendon in which the quadriceps fails to contract and the knee flexes through hamstring activation; it localises a lesion at the L2-L4 reflex arc (root, anterior horn or femoral nerve) together with pyramidal tract release above.
simple: When the doctor taps below the kneecap, the lower leg bends instead of kicking out. It means the nerve loop for the front thigh muscle is broken at the lumbar level while the spinal pathways above are overactive.
th: รีเฟล็กซ์หัวเข่ากลับด้าน เมื่อเคาะเอ็นสะบ้าแล้วเข่างอแทนที่จะเหยียด เกิดจากวงจรรีเฟล็กซ์ L2-L4 ขาด ทำให้ quadriceps ไม่หดตัว ขณะที่ทางเดิน pyramidal เหนือระดับนั้นปล่อยให้ hamstrings ไวเกิน ช่วยบอกระดับรอยโรคในไขสันหลังหรือราก
exam: With the patient seated and the leg relaxed, tap the patellar tendon firmly with a reflex hammer and watch both the quadriceps and the hamstring tendons. In an inverted response the knee flexes, often with a visible hamstring contraction, rather than extending. Compare sides, check for adductor spread and clonus, and test the ankle jerk and plantar responses.
pos: An inverted knee jerk localises to a segmental lesion at L2-L4 (nerve root, anterior horn or femoral nerve) with coexisting pyramidal hyperreflexia, for example a thoracic myelopathy with superimposed radiculopathy from a compressive or vascular lesion. It has been reported with a spinal epidural arteriovenous fistula and with compressive cord disease at the conus level. Look for MRI T2 cord signal, flow voids and arterial or compressive causes.

det.mechanism: Tapping the patellar tendon normally stretches the quadriceps spindle afferents (L2-L4) and triggers monosynaptic contraction. When this arc is interrupted, the quadriceps cannot respond. Pyramidal release from a lesion above lowers the threshold in adjacent segments, so the stretch spreads to the hamstrings (L5-S2) and the knee flexes.
det.technique: Seat the patient with the leg hanging relaxed, tap the tendon briskly and watch both the thigh extensors and flexors. Compare sides and note spread to the adductors, crossed reflexes and clonus. Test the ankle jerk and plantar response to place the lesion.
det.interpretation: It indicates a combined lesion: a segmental L2-L4 lesion (root, anterior horn or femoral nerve) plus upper motor neuron hyperreflexia, typically seen in thoracic or conus-level cord disease with root involvement. Reported causes include spinal vascular malformations and compressive myelopathy. Pure femoral neuropathy gives an absent, not inverted, reflex.
pearls: Knee flexes on patellar tap + spastic legs = think L2-L4 root/cord level plus cord disease above.
Look for a vascular shunt when MRI shows long T2 signal with flow voids.

name: Post-Exercise Reflex Facilitation
formal: Reappearance or marked increase of a depressed or absent tendon reflex after a brief (about 10 second) maximal voluntary contraction of the tested muscle; a bedside counterpart of the post-exercise facilitation and increment seen in presynaptic neuromuscular transmission disorders, for example Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
simple: A reflex that is absent at rest comes back, or becomes stronger, after the patient squeezes or pushes hard for about ten seconds. It points to a problem with release of acetylcholine at the nerve ending, as in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
th: รีเฟล็กซ์ที่ลดลงหรือหายไปขณะพักกลับปรากฏหรือแรงขึ้นหลังให้ผู้ป่วยเกร็งกล้ามเนื้อเต็มที่ประมาณ 10 วินาที เป็นสัญญาณของความผิดปกติก่อนไซแนปส์ที่ neuromuscular junction เช่น Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
exam: Test the patellar or ankle reflex at rest and record absence or weakness. Then ask the patient to contract the muscle maximally against resistance for about 10 seconds, release, and test the reflex immediately again. Compare the response before and after. Strength may also improve transiently, and electrodiagnosis shows an increment of more than 100 per cent after brief exercise.
pos: A depressed reflex that returns after brief exercise strongly suggests a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder, with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome the prototype. Combined with proximal weakness, dysautonomia and positive voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies it supports the diagnosis and should trigger a search for small cell lung cancer. Failure to facilitate does not exclude it, and neuropathy and myopathy do not show this change.

det.mechanism: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels reduce acetylcholine quanta released per impulse. A brief maximal contraction produces rapid firing, which lets calcium accumulate in the terminal and temporarily increases transmitter release. This restores muscle activation and with it the reflex response.
det.technique: Test the reflex at rest, ask for a maximal contraction of the same muscle for about 10 seconds, then re-test immediately. Repeated testing after a rest period shows the response fading again. Nerve conduction studies document the electrical counterpart as an increment above 100 per cent.
det.interpretation: Reflex return after brief exercise supports a presynaptic junction disorder and is a useful bedside clue to Lambert-Eaton syndrome, particularly with proximal weakness, dry mouth and autonomic dysfunction. It is not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose alone, so confirm with antibodies and neurophysiology and screen for malignancy.
pearls: Absent reflex that returns after 10 seconds of effort = think presynaptic NMJ disorder.
In myasthenia gravis, reflexes are usually preserved and exercise worsens strength.

name: Facial-Faucial-Finger Myoclonus
formal: Distinctive pattern of brief, jerky or tremulous movements of the eyelids and lower face, soft palate (faucial region) and fingers in juvenile-onset parkinsonism, characteristic of Kufor-Rakeb syndrome (ATP13A2 variants); surface EMG may show both myoclonic bursts shorter than 50 ms and more sustained tremulous bursts.
simple: Quick twitches that involve the eyelids and mouth area, the back of the throat and the fingers in a teenager or young adult with stiffness and slowness. It is a clue to a rare inherited form of early parkinsonism.
th: การกระตุกสั้นๆ หรือสั่นละเอียดที่หนังตา ใบหน้าส่วนล่าง เพดานอ่อน (faucial) และนิ้วมือ ในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินโซนิซึมเริ่มอายุน้อย เป็นลักษณะเด่นของ Kufor-Rakeb syndrome จากยีน ATP13A2 ซึ่งอาจมีทั้งส่วนของ myoclonus และ tremor ผสมกัน
exam: Observe the face at rest and during sustained posture for repeated small jerks of the orbicularis oculi, perioral muscles and the soft palate, and look at outstretched fingers for fine irregular twitching. Surface EMG over orbicularis oculi, extensor and flexor carpi radialis can separate synchronous bursts shorter than 50 ms from rhythmic tremulous bursting. Document with video.
pos: In a juvenile with levodopa-responsive parkinsonism, dystonia, pyramidal signs, supranuclear upgaze palsy or cognitive decline, this pattern supports Kufor-Rakeb syndrome and should prompt ATP13A2 testing. It helps to separate the disorder from other early-onset parkinsonism such as Parkin-related disease. It is not specific, and other causes of facial myoclonus should be excluded.

det.mechanism: ATP13A2 encodes a lysosomal P5-type ATPase, and loss of function disrupts lysosomal and mitochondrial handling of metals and alpha-synuclein. The resulting basal ganglia and pyramidal degeneration produce the characteristic cranial and distal myoclonus. Surface EMG shows both short myoclonic bursts and more sustained tremulous activity, so the movement is hybrid.
det.technique: Observe the face during rest, sustained posture and speech, and check the soft palate with the mouth open. Observe the outstretched fingers for fine twitching. Video and surface EMG help to document it.
det.interpretation: In an adolescent or young adult with dystonia-parkinsonism, pyramidal signs and upgaze palsy, the triad of eyelid-face, palate and finger twitching suggests Kufor-Rakeb syndrome. Other early-onset parkinsonism is more often Parkin related and lacks this pattern. Confirm with ATP13A2 sequencing.
pearls: Juvenile parkinsonism + eyelid-face-palate-finger twitching = think ATP13A2.
Surface EMG can show both myoclonic and tremulous bursts.
det.thd: Facial-faucial-finger myoclonus คือการกระตุกหรือสั่นละเอียดที่หนังตา ใบหน้า เพดานอ่อน และนิ้วมือ ในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินโซนิซึมวัยรุ่น เป็นเบาะแสของ Kufor-Rakeb syndrome (ATP13A2) ซึ่งมักมีสัญญาณ pyramidal และตามองขึ้นไม่ได้ร่วมด้วย ยืนยันด้วยยีน ATP13A2

name: Upbeat Nystagmus
formal: Vertical jerk nystagmus in primary gaze with a downward slow drift and upward fast phase, usually increasing on upgaze; it indicates bilateral central lesions of the pathways for vertical gaze holding and vertical vestibulo-ocular signals, most often in the paramedian caudal medulla, pontomesencephalic tegmentum or anterior vermis.
simple: The eyes keep drifting down and flicking back up while looking straight ahead. It always means a problem inside the brainstem or cerebellum, for example a small stroke, MS plaque or vitamin B1 deficiency.
th: ตากระตุกแนวตั้งในตำแหน่งมองตรง โดยตาค่อยๆ ลอยลงแล้วกระตุกกลับขึ้นอย่างเร็ว มักเพิ่มขึ้นเมื่อมองขึ้น บ่งบอกรอยโรคส่วนกลางในก้านสมองส่วน medulla, pons-midbrain หรือ vermis ของสมองน้อย สาเหตุเช่น หลอดเลือดสมอง MS เนื้องอก และ Wernicke encephalopathy
exam: Observe the eyes in primary gaze, then in up-, down- and lateral gaze, at near and distance; remove fixation with Frenzel or video goggles or watch the optic disc with an ophthalmoscope (the disc moves opposite to the eye's direction, so upbeat appears as downbeat at the disc). Check whether head tilt or lying supine changes it, test vertical pursuit, saccades and convergence, and look for internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Ask about oscillopsia and observe stance for backward falls.
pos: Primary-position upbeat nystagmus localises centrally: paramedian caudal medulla near the perihypoglossal nuclei, pontomesencephalic tegmentum or brachium conjunctivum, or the anterior vermis. Common causes are brainstem infarction, multiple sclerosis (often with INO), tumour, Wernicke encephalopathy, cerebellar degeneration and drug or alcohol toxicity. Acute cases usually fade over weeks; symptomatic oscillopsia may improve with aminopyridines in some patients. Small upbeat jerks only on extreme upgaze or under the influence of sedatives have less localising value.

det.mechanism: Holding the eyes steady in vertical gaze depends on a balance between upward and downward vestibular drives and on the vertical gaze-holding integrator. Upward vestibular signals from the anterior canals travel partly through the ventral tegmental tract and the medial longitudinal fascicle, and paramedian medullary neurons near the perihypoglossal nucleus feed the flocculus. Damage to these paths creates a downward bias, so the eyes drift down and are reset upward by quick phases. Otolith input may modulate it, which is why head position or lying down can change its intensity.
det.technique: Look for the nystagmus in primary gaze with and without fixation, and in upgaze, where it typically increases. Viewing the optic disc with an ophthalmoscope while the other eye is covered reveals low-amplitude nystagmus, remembering that the disc moves opposite to the cornea. Check for INO, vertical pursuit deficits, and backward falls on Romberg testing.
det.interpretation: Upbeat nystagmus in primary gaze is always central and less common than downbeat nystagmus. It suggests paramedian medullary, pontomesencephalic or anterior vermis lesions, commonly from stroke, MS, tumour or Wernicke encephalopathy, and is usually transient after acute lesions. Upbeat nystagmus combined with a unilateral or bilateral INO strongly suggests a pontomesencephalic MS plaque or paramedian infarct.
pearls: Primary-position upbeat nystagmus = central lesion; image the brainstem.
Alcohol misuse or poor nutrition with upbeat nystagmus: give thiamine before glucose.
Unlike downbeat nystagmus, upbeat nystagmus after acute lesions usually resolves within weeks.

name: HINTS Plus Examination
formal: Three-step bedside eye examination for patients with acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo, nausea, nystagmus and gait unsteadiness) - the Head Impulse, a check of Nystagmus for a change of direction with eccentric gaze, and the Test of Skew - with 'plus' adding a bedside test of new unilateral hearing loss; any central feature (normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation or new hearing loss) suggests stroke.
simple: A quick set of eye tests for someone with sudden, constant dizziness. If the head-turn test is abnormal, the eye jerks always beat the same way, and the eyes are level, it is probably an inner-ear problem. If any test points the other way, or hearing is newly lost on one side, think of a stroke.

exam: Use only in a patient who is currently dizzy with spontaneous nystagmus (acute vestibular syndrome), not in episodic or positional vertigo. 1) Head impulse: with the patient fixing on your nose, give small, fast, unpredictable horizontal head turns to each side and watch for a corrective catch-up saccade. 2) Nystagmus: examine in primary and right and left gaze; peripheral nystagmus beats in one direction and increases toward the fast phase, whereas direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus or pure vertical/torsional nystagmus is central. 3) Test of skew: alternate cover test looking for a vertical refixation movement. Plus: finger rub or bedside hearing test, ideally confirmed by audiogram. Add gait (can the patient stand or walk unaided?).
pos: Reassuring peripheral pattern = abnormal head impulse on one side + unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus + no skew + no new hearing loss. Any of: bilaterally normal head impulse, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, skew deviation, or new unilateral hearing loss points to brainstem or cerebellar stroke (AICA infarction can damage the labyrinth and give an abnormal head impulse with hearing loss). In expert hands the bundle detects posterior circulation stroke more sensitively than early diffusion MRI, which can miss small infarcts in the first 48 hours; performance falls in untrained users. Severe truncal ataxia is itself a central warning sign.

det.mechanism: A peripheral vestibular lesion reduces the vestibulo-ocular reflex on one side, so a fast head turn toward that side carries the eyes off target and a catch-up saccade follows; the resulting nystagmus beats away from the lesion and obeys Alexander's law without changing direction. Central lesions in the brainstem or cerebellum often spare the reflex arc, so the head impulse is normal, but they can impair gaze holding (direction-changing nystagmus) and the graviceptive otolith pathways (skew deviation). The AICA supplies both the labyrinth and the lateral pons and cerebellum, so new hearing loss with vertigo suggests vascular inner-ear and brainstem damage.
det.technique: Apply only to acute continuous vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus. Keep head turns small (10-20 degrees), fast and unpredictable in direction with the patient fixing on the examiner's nose; examine gaze to each side and check the alternate cover test for a vertical shift. Test hearing at the bedside and record gait. Video head-impulse devices can make the head impulse more reliable.
det.interpretation: A fully peripheral pattern (abnormal head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus, no skew, no new hearing loss) makes stroke unlikely in trained hands. Any central component, or inability to stand or walk, requires urgent stroke workup even if early diffusion MRI is normal, because small posterior circulation infarcts can be missed in the first 1-2 days. The test is not valid in patients without nystagmus or with episodic, positional or triggered dizziness, and accuracy depends heavily on examiner training.
pearls: INFARCT: Impulse Normal, Fast-phase Alternating, Refixation on Cover Test = central.
A normal head impulse in a patient with acute vertigo and nystagmus is a danger sign, not a reassuring one.
New unilateral hearing loss with acute vertigo may be AICA ischaemia even when the head impulse is abnormal.
